Chapter 4 • Tangent Spaces

4.3 Tensor Space \(T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\)

The concept of tensors generalizes that of vectors and covectors, providing a unified framework to describe multilinear geometric objects. While the definition of tensors is often introduced globally as tensor fields, it is conceptually clearer to begin with their local version at a point \(p \in \mathcal{M}\), constructed purely from the tangent and cotangent spaces \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) and \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\).

Tensors are often introduced as mysterious objects typically accompanied by the meaningless tautology “a tensor is an object that transforms like a tensor.” This unfortunate way of presenting tensors9 makes them appear more intimidating than they truly are. In reality, tensors are paper tigers.

  • Given a manifold \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A} \right)_d\), the \((r,s)\)-tensor space at \(p\) is the set of all multilinear maps of the form10 (Check Section 2.2 for the definition of multilinearity): \begin{align*} T \colon \underbrace{T_p^*\mathcal{M} \times \dots \times T_p^*\mathcal{M}}_{r \text{-times}} \times \underbrace{T_p\mathcal{M} \times \dots \times T_p\mathcal{M}}_{s \text{-times}} &\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \dots \\ \sim}} \mathbb{R} \\ \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}_{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}_{(s)} \right) &\longmapsto {T} \left( \mathsf{X}^{(1)}, \dots, \mathsf{X}^{(r)}, \mathcal{X}_{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}_{(s)} \right), \end{align*}

    Some particularly important cases of tensors are:

    • \((1, 0)\)-tensors: elements of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) (vectors).

    • \((0, 1)\)-tensors: elements of \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) (covectors).

    • \((0, 0)\)-tensors: real numbers, i.e., elements of \(\mathbb{R}\).

    • \((1, 1)\)-tensors: linear maps (matrices) from \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) to itself.

    • \((0, 2)\)-tensors: bilinear forms, such as the metric (more on this in Chapter 7).

  • Alternatively, using tensor products, the space \(T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\) can be defined algebraically as the vector space (see §2.2): \[ T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M} := \underbrace{T_p\mathcal{M} \otimes \dots \otimes T_p\mathcal{M}}_{r \text{-times}} \otimes \underbrace{T_p^*\mathcal{M} \otimes \dots \otimes T_p^*\mathcal{M}}_{s \text{-times}}. \]

  • Let \(\left\{ \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p \right\}\) and \(\left\{ (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right\}\) denote the bases of \(T_p\mathcal{M}\) and \(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\) associated with a chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) around \(p\), and let \(\left\{ \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i} \right)_p \right\}\) and \(\left\{ (d\mathscr{Y}^i)_p \right\}\) denote the corresponding bases associated with a different chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\).

    The components of a tensor \(T \in T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\) w.r.t. the chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\) are obtained by feeding it the basis elements of that chart, \[ \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s} \coloneqq T\left( (d\mathscr{X}^{i_1})_p, \dots, (d\mathscr{X}^{i_r})_p, \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_1}} \right)_p, \dots, \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_s}} \right)_p \right) \in \mathbb{R}, \] in terms of which the tensor is expanded as \[ T = \sum_{\substack{i_1,\dots,i_r \\ j_1,\dots,j_s}} \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}} \right)_p \otimes \dots \otimes \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_r}} \right)_p \otimes (d\mathscr{X}^{j_1})_p \otimes \dots \otimes (d\mathscr{X}^{j_s})_p. \] Denoting by \(\left( T_\mathcal{V} \right)^{k_1\dots k_r}_{l_1\dots l_s}\) the components w.r.t. the chart \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\), the transformation law for the components reads: \[ \left( T_\mathcal{U} \right)^{i_1\dots i_r}_{j_1\dots j_s} = \sum_{\substack{k_1,\dots,k_r \\ l_1,\dots,l_s}} \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{k_1}} \right)_p \cdots \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_r}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{k_r}} \right)_p \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{l_1}}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_1}} \right)_p \cdots \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^{l_s}}{\partial \mathscr{X}^{j_s}} \right)_p \cdot \left( T_\mathcal{V} \right)^{k_1\dots k_r}_{l_1\dots l_s}. \] As we saw in Subsections 4.1.1 and 4.2.1, each upper index (one per covector slot) transforms contravariantly, like the components of a vector, with a factor \(\left( \partial \mathscr{X}^{i} / \partial \mathscr{Y}^{k} \right)_p\), and each lower index (one per vector slot) transforms covariantly, like the components of a covector, with a factor \(\left( \partial \mathscr{Y}^{l} / \partial \mathscr{X}^{j} \right)_p\).

    By construction, the dimension of \(T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M}\) is \(\dim T_p^{(r,s)}\mathcal{M} = d^{r+s}\).

9

Common in many physics texts, perhaps stemming from the authors’ own apprehension toward differential geometry— a subject which, as the reader may have hopefully realized by this point, is in fact both harmless and remarkably beautiful.

10

The indices enclosed in parentheses, such as \(\mathsf{X}^{(i)}\) or \(\mathcal{X}_{(j)}\), refer strictly to the position of the argument within the tensor map \(T\). They are not to be confused with coordinate indices or component labels. This is a purely positional convention used for clarity when expressing properties like multilinearity.
